doc.title: Steve Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 25, 2002

title: His own piece Q-B-Rab and its title
summary: Listening to his own records, the barbecue title taken from Bobby Seale, and Nicholas Payton.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well I have one more thing here which I’m sure you’ll recognize.
Do you listen to your own records very often?
Not very often, only because I’m too self critical of my own, thinking oh if only I could have done this, or what was I thinking about, why did I play that, oh why did I sound that way?
I mean you were after that, right? That kind of that little dissonant thing there?
Oh yeah, yeah. Actually I was very happy with the way this particular cut came out though.
Yeah. Yeah. There’s a little story in the title of that and of course it’s called “Q-B-Rab,” which barbecue spelled backwards.

Yeah. And of course there’s a couple of different connections to that. Of course it’s a second line beat, which of course is from New Orleans so you can think about “Strutting with some Barbecue,” of course a little homage to Louis Armstrong. But the actual title came from, I got it from a book from Bobby Seale who was of course the former Black Panther and later on became the professor at Temple University. And for a while he became famous for his barbecue recipes. And he had a book called Q-B-Rab with Bobby Seale.

So here we have a second line rhythm in an odd meter. So you can think about the barbecue part but with a little twist on it, you know, Q-B-Rab. So that’s kind of the connection with the title. And of course Nicholas Payton being from New Orleans, I had him in mind when I wrote this piece.
